analysis.one_liner: Sets national rules for product-injury lawsuits, capping jury awards and shielding implant-material suppliers.
analysis.headline: A product-liability bill introduced with bipartisan sponsorship was placed on the Senate calendar in June 1998 and never received a vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the 50 states' product-liability laws with one federal set of rules for people injured by defective products. It would cap punitive damages, cut off lawsuits filed more than two years after an injury is discovered, shield business equipment from claims after 18 years, and make raw-material suppliers for medical implants almost impossible to sue. Supporters said this would lower product prices and keep suppliers from fleeing the market; the trade-off is that people hurt by dangerous products would have weaker and shorter-lived legal claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, product sellers, and raw-material suppliers for medical implants gain the most: uniform national rules end the patchwork of state laws, punitive awards become much harder to win, and suppliers of implant materials get an effective near-immunity. Small businesses facing suit get punitive damages capped at the lesser of $250,000 or twice the compensatory award. Workers' compensation insurers gain a new right to recover benefit payments from manufacturers.

how_it_helps.text: Caps punitive damages for small businesses and local governments at the lesser of $250,000 or twice the compensatory award, and requires any punitive award to be proven by clear and convincing evidence of 'conscious, flagrant indifference' to safety [S3].

Makes a claimant's intoxication a complete defense if the claimant was more than 50 percent responsible for the harm, and cuts damages by the share attributable to misuse or alteration of the product [S3].
Bars lawsuits filed more than two years after the harm and its cause were or should have been discovered, and bars claims about durable business equipment delivered more than 18 years earlier [S3].
Limits the liability of non-manufacturer sellers to cases of negligent care, breach of an express warranty, or intentional wrongdoing [S3].

Bars lawsuits against suppliers of raw materials and parts for medical implants unless the supplier was the manufacturer or seller or delivered materials that violated contract specifications, with procedures for early dismissal and no discovery before dismissal [S3].

The bill's findings argue that inconsistent state laws raise costs, reduce product availability, and burden interstate commerce, and that suppliers had stopped selling materials for implants because of litigation fears [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products. They would face a two-year filing deadline, an 18-year cutoff for business equipment, a higher proof standard and caps on punitive damages, a complete defense for defendants when the claimant was intoxicated, and near-immunity for the companies that supply implant materials — while federal rules would preempt stronger remedies in states that currently offer more protection.

drawbacks.text: The two-year statute of limitations and the 18-year cutoff for durable goods used in business would end some valid claims, including slow-developing injuries discovered late [S3].
Biomaterials suppliers could be dismissed from implant lawsuits before any discovery, leaving injured patients to sue only the implant maker even where the supplier's material is at issue [S3].

Punitive damages — the main legal penalty for concealing known product dangers — would require clear-and-convincing proof of 'conscious, flagrant indifference,' a much higher bar than most state law [S3].
The bill preempts state product-liability law nationwide, so states whose courts have developed stronger consumer protections would lose them [S3].
A claimant under the influence of alcohol or drugs who was more than 50 percent responsible loses the entire case, even if the product was also defective [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real benefits to businesses: predictable national rules, lower litigation costs, and protection for small defendants facing outsized punitive awards, and it addresses a genuine shortage-of-suppliers problem for implant materials. But the costs are concentrated on exactly the people the tort system exists to compensate — those injured by dangerous products. The caps, deadlines, and supplier immunity would have weakened the main financial pressure that pushes manufacturers to make safer products, and federal preemption would override consumer protections in states that chose stronger ones. On balance this is a transfer of legal risk from manufacturers to injured consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business in June 1998 and sat there until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999, without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Slade Gorton introduced the bill in the Senate on June 25, 1998, joined by Democrats John Rockefeller and Joseph Lieberman [S3][S4].
It was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 441 on June 26, 1998 [S3][S5].
No committee is listed and no further action — no hearing, no floor debate, no vote — is recorded before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured consumers kept the full state-law remedies the bill would have trimmed, and the plaintiffs' trial bar kept its practice. Manufacturers, sellers, and implant-material suppliers got none of the new limits they sought, but also suffered no change to the status quo.

for.name: Slade Gorton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Product Liability Reform Act of 1998 and placed it on the Senate calendar

for.name: John Rockefeller
for.what_they_did: Joined Gorton in introducing the bill

for.name: Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Joined Gorton in introducing the bill

for.name: Manufacturing, retail, and medical-implant supplier interests
for.role: Business coalition favoring federal tort limits
for.what_they_did: Backed federal product-liability caps and the biomaterials supplier immunity; such coalitions had pushed similar bills in prior Congresses

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and floor schedulers
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor debate or a vote after placing it on the calendar; the bill died there when the Congress ended

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Had vetoed a nearly identical product-liability bill in 1996, making any similar bill face an almost certain veto

against.name: Trial lawyers and consumer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal caps on product-liability awards and preemption of state tort law

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with three Democratic cosponsors — but the bill never reached a floor vote, so the chamber's actual partisan split was never recorded.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of consumer and business products
industries.note: The bill caps punitive exposure, sets proof deadlines, and creates intoxication and misuse defenses, shifting legal risk from manufacturers to injured consumers. Higher proof standards for punitive damages also weaken the deterrent against concealing known product dangers.

industries.industry: Medical implant makers and biomaterials suppliers
industries.note: Title II makes raw-material and component suppliers for implants effectively unsuable except for violating contract specifications, with mandatory early dismissal and no discovery first. Suppliers gain lawsuit protection; patients harmed by implants lose a path to recovery against the material maker.

Sellers would be liable only for their own negligence, express warranties, or intentional wrongdoing, rather than being held responsible for defective products they merely sold or rented. The saving would come out of injured buyers' recoveries.
Shorter deadlines, caps, and dismissal procedures shrink the caseload and the recoveries that fund contingency-fee suits. Their interest runs with injured clients who would have weaker claims.

industries.industry: Workers' compensation insurers and self-insured employers
industries.note: The bill grants insurers a subrogation right to recover benefit payments from manufacturers and a voice in litigation over employer fault — new recovery rights — while the employer-fault provisions also give defendants a route to reduce damages. Gains and costs pull in both directions for this group.
